question.worked_solution:
The first thing we notice is that we can rewrite the terms of the series as powers of $\frac{5}{9}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\frac{5}{9}+\frac{25}{81}+⋯+\frac{{5}^{n}}{{9}^{n}}+⋯ & =1+\frac{{5}^{1}}{{9}^{1}}+\frac{{5}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}+⋯+\frac{{5}^{n}}{{9}^{n}}+⋯ \\  & =1+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{1}+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{2}+⋯+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x)=\frac{1}{1-x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1-x} & =1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯+{x}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{5}{9}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(1-\frac{5}{9})} & =1+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{1}+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{2}+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{3}+⋯+{(\frac{5}{9})}^{n}+⋯ \\ \frac{9}{4} & =1+\frac{5}{9}+\frac{25}{81}+\frac{125}{729}+⋯+\frac{{5}^{n}}{{9}^{n}}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\frac{9}{4}.$
